title: NASA Invites Blue Origin to Test New Glenn Rocket at Historic Stennis Space Center After Launch Pad Explosion
excerpt: The partnership gives Blue Origin access to the Apollo-era B-2 test stand in Mississippi for upper-stage hot-fire testing, as repairs continue at its damaged Cape Canaveral launch complex following a catastrophic May explosion.
body:
• NASA and Blue Origin signed an agreement to test the New Glenn rocket's second stage at the B-2 test stand at Stennis Space Center in Mississippi.
  • The partnership follows the catastrophic May 28 explosion that destroyed a New Glenn booster and severely damaged Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral.
  • Testing at Stennis is targeted to begin this fall, supporting Artemis lunar missions planned for 2027 and beyond.
  • The B-2 stand previously tested Saturn V stages for Apollo and hosted the Space Launch System Green Run campaign for Artemis I.

NASA and Blue Origin have formalized an agreement to conduct hot-fire testing of the New Glenn rocket's second stage at one of the space agency's most historic facilities, a strategic pivot that comes after the spectacular destruction of a New Glenn booster on its Florida launch pad in May.

Under the arrangement, announced July 24, Blue Origin will use the B-2 position of the Thad Cochran Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Testing is targeted to begin this fall.

From Apollo to Artemis

The B-2 stand carries a lineage that stretches back to the dawn of human space exploration. Built in the 1960s, it was originally constructed to test Saturn V rocket stages that carried American astronauts to the Moon during the Apollo program. More recently, it hosted the Green Run test series of the Space Launch System core stage ahead of the Artemis I mission.

"Stennis helped take Americans to the Moon, and through this partnership, it will take us back," said Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp.

"Winning the new space race means moving faster and working alongside a strong commercial industry. Supporting Blue Origin at NASA's Stennis Space Center puts world-class American infrastructure to work advancing the capabilities needed to return astronauts to the Moon."

— Jared Isaacman, NASA Administrator

Rebuilding After the Explosion

The agreement is an annex to a reimbursable Space Act Agreement signed earlier in July. It comes directly in the wake of the May 28, 2026, explosion at Cape Canaveral's Launch Complex 36, where a New Glenn booster designated "No, It's Necessary" erupted in a fireball during a static-fire engine test.

The explosion destroyed the rocket, severely damaged the transporter-erector, toppled one of the pad's two towers, and left the launch complex in need of extensive repairs. NASA Administrator Isaacman said at the time that pad repairs could take "serious time," with a 2028 timeline "within the realm" of possibility.

No injuries were reported in the incident. The booster had been preparing for its fourth flight, which was to deliver 48 Amazon Leo satellites into low-Earth orbit.

The Second Stage at Stennis

The New Glenn second stage, designated GS2, is powered by two BE-3U engines burning liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, producing a combined 400,000 pounds of thrust in vacuum. Under the agreement, NASA will supply engineers, specialized equipment, and facility modifications to prepare the B-2 stand for testing.

Blue Origin framed the Stennis arrangement as part of a broader effort to add test capacity and reduce pressure on its Florida operations. The company holds contracts for both a robotic lunar delivery mission and a human landing system for later Artemis flights.

What's at Stake for Artemis

New Glenn is central to several upcoming NASA missions. The rocket is slated to launch Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 Endurance lander later this year, carrying NASA payloads to the lunar south pole. That mission is designed to retire risk ahead of crewed landings planned under Artemis IV and V in 2028.

The explosion came just two days after NASA awarded Blue Origin a $188 million contract to deliver lunar rovers to the Moon's surface, and less than a week after SpaceX — years ahead in development — conducted a largely successful test of its next-generation Starship rocket.

For the Indian space community watching from ISRO and the private sector, the New Glenn saga illustrates both the enormous difficulty of developing heavy-lift launch capability and the resilience of the partnerships that sustain it.
